name: Mechanical horse

image.caption: Micke on a mechanical exercise horse.

lead: A mechanical horse is a device that mimics the movement of a real horse, from riding simulators used in rehabilitation and jockey training to bucking machines used by rodeo riders. Using one asks the rider to keep the trunk upright and balanced against constant three-dimensional movement.
That trunk work is why it comes up in core and posture training. Studies have looked at balance in patients with stroke and cerebral palsy, and at the physical demands of racing on a simulator.

paras: The user sits astride and the machine produces forward-back, side-to-side and up-down movement at adjustable speeds, while the rider stabilises the trunk. Sessions are typically supervised in clinics or training facilities.
Rodeo-style bucking machines can cause falls and injuries; simulators are lower-risk but are used under supervision in clinical settings.

chain: Trunk and pelvis stabilise against it
Better balance and trunk control, supporting upright posture
angle.text: Riding a mechanical horse engages the trunk and pelvic muscles to stay balanced. People use it to train core control and posture.

lead: Mechanical horse-riding simulators are devices that mimic real horse movement, generating many three-dimensional movements: forward and back, left and right, up and down [1]. They are used in neurological rehabilitation, in jockey training, and in research on postural control [1][2].

In appearance terms, the draw is core engagement: the rider's trunk and pelvis must continually adjust to the movement, which is described as a perturbation-training stimulus [3]. Better trunk control and balance contribute to posture and a stronger midsection.
Rodeo practice machines are a related category: mechanical bulls grew out of the bucking barrel and have long been used to train rodeo riders [4].

paras: Simulators mimic equine movement, typically with adjustable frequency [1][3]. A study of healthy participants on a horse simulator found head and trunk responses were highly specific to the direction and frequency of the movement, and that adding pelvic straps and trunk support changed responses [3].

A 2019 meta-analysis of simulators for postural balance in neurological rehabilitation found favourable results for balance in stroke patients on the Berg Balance Scale, with inconclusive results for sitting balance in cerebral palsy and a limited number of studies [1]. A 2022 review of 10 trials in 343 patients with cerebral palsy compared simulator therapy plus physiotherapy with physiotherapy alone [2].

In 18 trainee jockeys, a race simulation on a mechanical racing simulator reached a mean peak oxygen uptake of about 43 ml per kg per minute, around 75 percent of peak [5]. A study comparing riders and non-riders on a simulator found riders had lower postural displacements [6].

The mechanical bull developed from the bucking barrel, and was popularised as entertainment by the 1980 film Urban Cowboy; injuries are described as relatively rare but include falls and being thrown [4].
